html:
The House of Wisdom, Bayt al-Hikma in Arabic, was the library of the Abbasid caliphs in Baghdad from around 800, where scholars copied, translated and studied books. Later tradition made it a grand academy; historians now see it more as a palace library and workshop whose fame grew in the telling.

It grew out of the book collecting of Harun al-Rashid and flourished under his son al-Ma'mun, who ruled from 813 to 833. It was at the heart of the translation movement, which put works by Aristotle, Galen, Euclid and Ptolemy into Arabic, often through Syriac, along with Persian and Indian texts. Cheap paper, newly made in Baghdad, helped.

Scholars tied to it include al-Khwarizmi, whose book on algebra gave the subject its name, and the translator Hunayn ibn Ishaq. Tradition says the library was destroyed when the Mongols sacked Baghdad in 1258 and its books thrown into the Tigris. The name still stands for an age of learning; the founders of Saudi Arabia's KAUST spoke of reviving it.
